Working-class women activists were central to the expansion of civil society and citizenship in Britain in the first half and half of the twentieth-century, and that they achieved social reforms, such as free school meals, that were both humane and inclusive.
Working class women in Britain during the period 1900 to 1948 were active in civil society, and their activism was a significant factor in the development of civil and social citizenship.
working class women were active in local civil society in Britain before the welfare state.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how working class women were able to create a civil society that promoted social citizenship and social welfare in the first half and half of the twentieth-century.
the ways in which working class women contributed to the development and expansion of citizenship at the local level, and with how they were affected by the development of the welfare state.
the role of women in local government and in voluntary organisations in Britain between 1880 and 1948.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
working class women's participation in civil society was a significant and important factor in the development of citizenship in Britain in the first half century.

the working class women who were active in local government and the Poor Law during the first half century of the twentieth century, and the working class women in the voluntary sector during the same period, were the most significant contributors to the development of a civil society that included working class women.

the working class women activists who were the subject of this essay were a vital part of the civil society that was so important in the development of citizenship in the first half twentieth century, and that they made a significant contribution to the development of a more democratic society.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have sought to recover the contribution made by working class women to the expansion of citizenship during the first half century of the twentieth century, and to argue that their activism in civil society was a more important influence than that of the central state.
working class women were central to the creation of a civil society in which citizenship was inclusive and active, and in which the local level was a central site for activism and reform.
the welfare state was not a benign development for working class women, but rather a mixed blessing.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the history of women’s political participation is more complex than the standard narrative of a linear progression towards equality, and that the history of the welfare state is also much more complex than the conventional story of its progressive development.
the history of working class women’s activism in the early twentieth century is not just a history of the welfare state, nor is it simply a story of the development of the women’s movement.
the welfare state was not a panacea, and that it did not necessarily enhance women’s citizenship.
